newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: U.N. evacuates convoy from Afghan town amid chaos.
newsitem.headline: U.N. evacuates convoy from Afghan town amid chaos.

text.p: A U.N. convoy evacuated aid workers and journalists from the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif to the border town of Uzbekistan amid violent scenes on Thursday, witnesses said.
The convoy of about 70 people left a day after local Afghan Uzbek and Shi'ite Moslem forces drove about 3,000 Islamic Taleban militiamen out of the northern Afghan capital in a bloody 15-hour battle.
Taleban corpses still lay in the streets of Mazar-i-Sharif, where charred vehicles and burned shops and buildings bore a witness to the intensity of the fire-fight that began on Tuesday.

The staff of the United Nations and other relief agencies, along with the western journalists, pulled away from the U.N. guest house for what is normally a one-hour drive to Heyretan town on the Uzbekistan border, 90 km (56 miles) to the north.
As soon as the 12-vehicle convoy left, crowds who had gathered to watch attacked and looted the guest house, briefly holding two U.N. international staff who had stayed behind.
Uzbek troops commanded by General Majid Rouzi, security chief of Mazar-i-Sharif, intervened and chased the looters, witnesses said.
His soldiers summarily executed one of the thieves in front of the guest house.
As the convoy drove out of the town, Uzbek troops were shifting about 200 black-bearded Taleban prisoners from two open trucks into a mud-walled prison, watched by crowds of residents.
Further along the road east of Mazar-i-Sharif, the convoy passed pick-up trucks of the International Committee of Red Cross (ICRC) that had recovered several bodies from the combat.

There was no other sign of the Taleban, who had retreated along the road to Pul-i-Khumri town in the northeastern province of Baghlan after being driven from Mazar-i-Sharif before the junction with the Heyretan road across the desert, about 60 km (37 miles) away.
At the border, a helicopter was flying on the Uzbek side of the Amu Darya (Oxus river) that marks the border.
Uzbek troops had blocked the Friendship Bridge with huge concrete blocks, barbed wire and machinegun emplacements.
Uzbek border guards had orders to prevent any Afghan or Pakistani nationals from crossing into Uzbekistan.
U.N. officials said a Pakistani delegation was on its way from Islamabad to Termez to try to negotiate safe passage for 13 evacuees from the Pakistani consulate in Mazar-i-Sharif.
Earlier on Thursday, life appeared to be returning to normal in the war-ravaged city, a day after the rout of its Taleban Islamic militia captors by local Afghan forces.
Shops reopened and people returned to the streets apparently happy by the retreat of the Taleban fighters only after 72 hours in the city.
Witnesses said bodies of Taleban fighters and burned-out trucks and other vehicles lay in the streets of the city, now firmly in control of ethnic Uzbek troops of General Abdul Malik.
Malik turned on the militia on Tuesday, only eight days after striking an alliance with them amid a mutiny he staged against opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who later fled to Turkey.
There were a few charred buildings and shops but there were more people on the streets than there had been before Mazar-i-Sharif fell to Malik's troops on Saturday.
"Shops are reopening, people are relaxed and happy that the Taleban are out of the town," a Mazar resident said.
In the Shi'ite Moslem district of Saidabad the bodies of eight Taleban fighters lay piled on the ground awaiting collection by an ICRC vehicle.
"This is what happens to every foreigner who comes to the north," Ahmed Ali, a resident of Saidabad, said.
Outside the foreign ministry in Mazar-i-Sharif, there were remnants of a truck whose cargo of ammunition had exploded during the battle.

"The Pakistanis were very happy when their ambassador came to Mazar, it was a celebration for Pakistan, now they are crying because of what happened to the Taleban," another resident, Amir Shah, said.
"All the people in the town were fighting the Taleban," he added.
Residents were visibly delighted to see the back of the Taleban, who only arrived on Sunday but wasted little time in trying to impose their strict version of Islam on the city.
Swarming through Mazar-i-Sharif in white-flagged vehicles, they broadcast orders that men should grow beards, women should stay at home and girls should stop going to school.
Another resident, Muhammad Zuhair, accused the militia of being supported by Pakistan and the United States.
"Our message to the United States, the Pakistanis and the Arabs is that don't interfere in Afghan affairs, let us make our own choice about our own government," Zuhair said.
Pakistan was the first of three countries to accord formal diplomatic recognition to the Taleban government after the capture of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The defeated Taleban left the city towards the southeast on Wednesday heading towards Pul-i-Khumri in Baghlan province and were chased by Malik's tanks and military vehicles.

Pul-i-Khumri, lying on the main highway from the capital Kabul to north Afghanistan via the strategic Salang Pass, was captured by the Taleban on Wednesday from forces of Syed Jafar Naderi, allied to the Dostum-led opposition alliance.
